summary: Discovery of Designated Resolvers (DDR) lets a client that only knows a resolver's IP address find that resolver's encrypted DNS settings using DNS records. It can move a client from unencrypted DNS to encrypted DNS. It is intended only for cases where the unencrypted resolver and its designated resolver are run by the same or cooperating entities.

plainLanguage.summary: Encrypted DNS needs more than an IP address: the server usually has a name, and it may listen on a special port or want a particular web path. RFC 9462 lets a device ask its plain DNS server, by name, for those details, and then check that the encrypted server it found really belongs to the same operator.

questions: discover doh endpoint from resolver ip
how does a client discover encrypted dns
subtitle: How a device that only knows a DNS server's IP address can find out whether that server offers encrypted DNS, and verify it.

tldr.problem: Networks usually hand out only the IP address of a DNS resolver, but encrypted DNS such as DoT, DoQ and DoH can need a hostname, other addresses, a non-standard port or a URI Template.
tldr.mechanism: The client asks the resolver for SVCB records at the special name _dns.resolver.arpa, or at _dns plus the resolver name when it knows the resolver's name. It then checks the TLS certificate before switching to the Designated Resolver it learned about.
tldr.outcome: A client can move from unencrypted to encrypted DNS automatically, but only to a resolver run by the same or a cooperating entity. On-path attackers can still block discovery.

today: RFC 9462 is a Proposed Standard, published in November 2023. No RFC obsoletes it and no RFC updates it. Its companion RFC 9463 defines DHCP and Router Advertisement options, and where both are present the network-designated information takes precedence, because it is considered the more reliable source.

sections.title: Finding the Encrypted DNS Service
sections.content:
When DNS clients wish to use encrypted DNS protocols such as DNS over TLS (RFC 7858), DNS over QUIC (RFC 9250), or DNS over HTTPS (RFC 8484), they can require additional information beyond the IP address of the DNS server, such as the resolver's hostname, alternate IP addresses, non-standard ports, or URI Templates. However, common configuration mechanisms only provide the resolver's IP address during configuration. Such mechanisms include network provisioning protocols like DHCP (RFC 2132, RFC 8415) and IPv6 Router Advertisement options (RFC 8106), as well as manual configuration.

This document defines two mechanisms for clients to discover Designated Resolvers that support these encrypted protocols using DNS server Service Binding (SVCB) records (RFC 9460). When only an IP address of an Unencrypted DNS Resolver is known, the client queries a Special-Use Domain Name (RFC 6761) to discover DNS SVCB records associated with one or more Encrypted DNS Resolvers that the Unencrypted DNS Resolver has designated for use when support for DNS encryption is requested. When the hostname of an Encrypted DNS Resolver is known, the client requests details by sending a query for a DNS SVCB record. This can be used to discover alternate encrypted DNS protocols supported by a known server, or to provide details if a resolver name is provisioned by a network.

Both approaches allow clients to confirm that a discovered Encrypted DNS Resolver is designated by the originally provisioned resolver. Designated in this context means that the resolvers are operated by the same entity or cooperating entities, for example because the resolvers are accessible on the same IP address, or because there is a certificate that contains the IP address for the original designating resolver.
sections.plainLanguage: The gap this fills is narrow but real. A network can hand a device an IP address and nothing else, and that is not enough to set up DoH. This RFC gives the device a standard question to ask so the answer comes back in DNS.

sections.title: The SVCB Records
sections.content:
DNS resolvers can advertise one or more Designated Resolvers that may offer support over encrypted channels and are controlled by the same entity. When a client discovers Designated Resolvers, it learns information such as the supported protocols and ports. This information is provided in ServiceMode SVCB records for DNS servers, although AliasMode SVCB records can be used to direct clients to the needed ServiceMode record. The formatting of these records, including the DNS-unique parameters such as dohpath, is defined by RFC 9461.

An example SVCB record describing a DoH server discovered by querying for _dns.example.net is _dns.example.net. 7200 IN SVCB 1 example.net. (alpn=h2 dohpath=/dns-query{?dns}). A DoT server is described as _dns.example.net. 7200 IN SVCB 1 dot.example.net (alpn=dot port=8530), and a DoQ server as _dns.example.net. 7200 IN SVCB 1 doq.example.net (alpn=doq port=8530). If multiple Designated Resolvers are available, using one or more encrypted DNS protocols, the resolver deployment can indicate a preference using the priority fields in each SVCB record.

If the client encounters a mandatory parameter in a SVCB record it does not understand, it MUST NOT use that record to discover a Designated Resolver. The client can still use other records in the same response if it understands all of their mandatory parameters. That allows future encrypted deployments to support several protocols at once even if a given client is not aware of all of them: a resolver returning three records, one for DoH, one for DoT and one for a protocol that does not exist yet, lets a client that supports only DoH and DoT use those two records while safely ignoring the third.

To avoid name lookup deadlock, clients that use Designated Resolvers need to ensure that a specific Encrypted DNS Resolver is not used for any queries needed to resolve the name of the resolver itself, or to perform certificate revocation checks for the resolver. Designated Resolvers need to ensure that this deadlock is avoidable as well.
sections.plainLanguage: Each encrypted service gets its own record, and the priority number says which to prefer. A client that meets a parameter it does not understand skips that one record rather than the whole answer, so a new protocol can be advertised without breaking older clients.

sections.title: Discovery from a Resolver IP Address
sections.content:
When a DNS client is configured with an Unencrypted DNS Resolver IP address, it SHOULD query the resolver for SVCB records of a service with a scheme of dns and an authority of resolver.arpa before making other queries. This allows the client to switch to using encrypted DNS for all other queries if possible. Specifically, the client issues a query for _dns.resolver.arpa. with the SVCB resource record type, 64.

Responses to the SVCB query for the resolver.arpa special-use domain describe Designated Resolvers. To ensure that different Designated Resolver configurations can be correctly distinguished and associated with the A and AAAA records for the resolver, ServiceMode SVCB responses to these queries MUST NOT use the . or resolver.arpa value for the TargetName, and clients MUST NOT perform A or AAAA queries for resolver.arpa.

If the recursive resolver that receives this query has one or more Designated Resolvers, it returns the corresponding SVCB records. When responding to these special queries, it SHOULD include the A and AAAA records for the name of the Designated Resolver in the Additional Answers section, which saves the client an additional round trip. Designated Resolvers SHOULD be accessible using the IP address families supported by their associated Unencrypted DNS Resolvers: if the unencrypted resolver is reachable over IPv4 it ought to provide an A record for an IPv4 address of the Designated Resolver, and the same for IPv6. The Designated Resolver MAY support more address families than the unencrypted resolver but SHOULD NOT support fewer. If the recursive resolver that receives the query has no Designated Resolvers, it SHOULD return NODATA for queries to the resolver.arpa zone, to give clients a consistent and accurate signal.

A client MAY use a discovered Designated Resolver without validation only on the basis of implementation-specific policy or user input. Clients MUST NOT automatically use a Designated Resolver without some sort of validation. Use without validation can allow an attacker to direct traffic to an Encrypted DNS Resolver unrelated to the original one. A client MUST NOT reuse a designation discovered using the IP address of one Unencrypted DNS Resolver in place of any other; the client needs to repeat the discovery process. Designations are per-resolver and MUST NOT be used to configure the client's universal DNS behaviour. If a client is configured with the same unencrypted resolver IP address on multiple different networks, a Designated Resolver discovered on one network SHOULD NOT be reused on any of the others without repeating discovery, since the same IP address may be used for different servers on different networks.
sections.plainLanguage: The client asks one specific question before it asks anything else, then uses the answer for the rest of its queries. The rule about repeating discovery on a new network matters: the same private IP address can mean a completely different resolver on a different network.

sections.title: Verified and Opportunistic Discovery
sections.content:
Verified Discovery is a mechanism that allows the automatic use of a Designated Resolver that supports DNS encryption and that performs a TLS handshake. To be considered a verified Designated Resolver, the TLS certificate it presents has to pass two checks made by the client. The client MUST verify the chain of certificates up to a trust anchor, as described in Section 6 of RFC 5280, and SHOULD use the default system or application trust anchors unless otherwise configured. The client MUST also verify that the certificate contains the IP address of the designating Unencrypted DNS Resolver in an iPAddress entry of the subjectAltName extension.

If these checks pass, the client SHOULD use the discovered Designated Resolver for any case in which it would have otherwise used the Unencrypted DNS Resolver, so as to prefer encrypted DNS whenever possible. If they fail, the client MUST NOT automatically use the discovered Designated Resolver if the designation was only discovered via a _dns.resolver.arpa. query, and it SHOULD suppress further queries for Designated Resolvers using that resolver for the length of time given by the SVCB record's time to live, to avoid excessive queries that will lead to further failed validations.

Opportunistic Discovery covers the cases where verified discovery is not possible, for example when the identities of resolvers on private IP addresses, Unique Local Addresses and link-local addresses cannot be safely confirmed using TLS certificates under most conditions. An opportunistic privacy profile is defined for DoT as a mode in which clients do not validate the name of the resolver presented in the certificate, and the same profile applies to DoQ. A client MAY use information from the SVCB record for _dns.resolver.arpa. with this opportunistic privacy profile as long as the IP address of the Encrypted DNS Resolver does not differ from the IP address of the Unencrypted DNS Resolver. Clients SHOULD use this mode only for resolvers using private or local IP addresses, since resolvers that use other addresses are able to provision TLS certificates for their addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: When the resolver has a public address, the client can check its certificate and see whether that certificate covers the address of the plain resolver it was given. If it does, the two are the same operator and the client can switch. When the address is private, that check is not possible, so the client may only use the encrypted resolver if it is at the very same address.

sections.title: Discovery from a Resolver Name
sections.content:
A DNS client that already knows the name of an Encrypted DNS Resolver can use DDR to discover details about all supported encrypted DNS protocols. This situation arises if a client has been configured to use a given Encrypted DNS Resolver, or if a network provisioning protocol such as DHCP or IPv6 Router Advertisements provides a name for an Encrypted DNS Resolver alongside the resolver IP address, for example by using Discovery of Network-designated Resolvers (RFC 9463).

For these cases the client simply sends a DNS SVCB query using the known name of the resolver. The query can be issued to the named Encrypted DNS Resolver itself or to any other resolver. Unlike the case of bootstrapping from an Unencrypted DNS Resolver, these records SHOULD be available in the public DNS if the same domain name's A or AAAA records are available in the public DNS, to allow using any resolver to discover another resolver's Designated Resolvers. When the name can only be resolved in private namespaces, these records SHOULD be available to the same audience as the A and AAAA records.

For example, if the client already knows about a DoT server resolver.example.com, it can issue a SVCB query for _dns.resolver.example.com to discover whether other encrypted DNS protocols are available. The answer would be _dns.resolver.example.com. 7200 IN SVCB 1 resolver.example.com. (alpn=h2 dohpath=/dns-query{?dns}) and _dns.resolver.example.com. 7200 IN SVCB 2 resolver.example.com. (alpn=dot), indicating that both DoH and DoT are supported and that the DoH server has the higher priority.

Clients MUST validate that for any Encrypted DNS Resolver discovered using a known resolver name, the TLS certificate of the resolver contains the known name in a subjectAltName extension. Both servers in the example need certificates that cover resolver.example.com. Often the various supported encrypted DNS protocols are specified so that the SVCB TargetName matches the known name, as in the example, but even when the TargetName is different, for example a DoH server with a TargetName of doh.example.com, the clients still check for the original known resolver name in the certificate. This resolver validation is not related to the DNS resolver that provided the SVCB answer.
sections.plainLanguage: If you already know a resolver's name, you can ask for its details the same way. The check is slightly different: the certificate has to contain the name you started with, not an address.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because clients can receive DNS SVCB answers over unencrypted DNS, on-path attackers can prevent successful discovery by dropping SVCB queries or answers, and so can prevent clients from switching to encrypted DNS. Clients should be aware that it may not be possible to distinguish between a resolver that has no Designated Resolver and such an active attack. To limit the impact of discovery queries being dropped, clients can re-send their SVCB queries periodically. Another kind of downgrade attack blocks connections to the encrypted DNS server, and for DDR clients need to validate a Designated Resolver using a connection to the server before trusting it, so attackers who can block those connections can also prevent the switch.

Encrypted DNS Resolvers that allow discovery using DNS SVCB answers over unencrypted DNS MUST NOT provide differentiated behaviour based solely on metadata in the SVCB record, such as the HTTP path or an alternate port number, because those are parameters an attacker could modify. For example, if a DoH resolver provides a filtering service for one URI path and a non-filtered service for another, an attacker could select which of those services is used by modifying the dohpath parameter. These attacks can be mitigated by providing separate resolver IP addresses or hostnames.

While the IP address of the Unencrypted DNS Resolver is often provisioned over insecure mechanisms, it can also be provisioned securely, such as by manual configuration, on a VPN, or on a network with protections like RA-Guard. An attacker might try to direct encrypted DNS traffic to itself by causing the client to think that a discovered Designated Resolver uses a different IP address from the Unencrypted DNS Resolver. If the IP address of a Designated Resolver differs from that of an Unencrypted DNS Resolver, clients applying Verified Discovery MUST validate that the IP address of the Unencrypted DNS Resolver is covered by the SubjectAltName of the Designated Resolver's TLS certificate, and if that validation fails the client MUST NOT automatically use the discovered Designated Resolver.

Clients using Opportunistic Discovery MUST be limited to cases where the Unencrypted DNS Resolver and the Designated Resolver have the same IP address, which SHOULD be a private or local IP address. Clients that do not follow Opportunistic Discovery and instead try to connect without first checking for a designation run the risk of being intercepted by an attacker hosting an Encrypted DNS Resolver on an IP address of an Unencrypted DNS Resolver where the attacker has failed to gain control of the Unencrypted DNS Resolver.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything here travels over plain DNS, so someone on the path can simply drop the answer and the client stays on unencrypted DNS without noticing. The certificate check is what stops them from redirecting the client to their own encrypted server instead.
